exercises.title: Design Dynamic Array (Vector)

hints.title: Capacity vs Size Tracking
hints.content_markdown: Keep track of two distinct variables: `length` (current count of stored items) and `capacity` (allocated heap buffer size). When `length == capacity`, double the capacity.

hints.title: Geometric Growth & Memory Management
hints.content_markdown:
1. Initialize with `new int[capacity]`.
2. In `push_back`: if `length == capacity`, allocate `new int[capacity * 2]`, copy old elements over, deallocate old buffer with `delete[] data`, and point `data` to new buffer.
3. In destructor `~DynamicArray()`: execute `delete[] data` to avoid leaks.

hints.title: Class Implementation Blueprint

exercises.title: Design a Dynamic Array (Vector)
exercises.time_complexity_target: O(1) amortized append, O(1) random access

hints.title: Nudge
hints.content_markdown: Two variables, not one: `length` is how many elements are stored, `capacity` is how many the buffer holds. They are equal exactly once per doubling, and that is the entire amortized argument.

hints.title: Strategy
hints.content_markdown:
1. Allocate the buffer on the heap in the constructor and remember the requested capacity.
2. In `push_back`, when `length == capacity`, allocate a buffer of twice the capacity, copy the live elements across, release the old buffer, and bump the resize counter.
3. `get` and `set` must reject indices outside `[0, length)`; `pop_back` must reject an empty array. Both throw `std::out_of_range`.
4. The destructor releases the buffer. Delete the copy constructor and copy assignment, or the raw pointer will be freed twice.

hints.title: Method blueprint
hints.content_markdown:
For each method, write its **signature and a one-line comment saying what it guarantees** -- no bodies.

- `explicit DynamicArray(int cap = 2)` -- heap buffer, length 0, resize count 0; non-positive `cap` becomes 2.
- `~DynamicArray()` -- releases the buffer.
- `void push_back(int n)` -- grows the buffer if full, then stores.
- `int pop_back() const -> int` (no; `int pop_back()`) -- returns the last element, shrinking length.
- `int get(int i) const` / `void set(int i, int n)` -- bounds-checked element access.
- `int size() const` / `int get_capacity() const` / `int resizes() const` -- O(1) accessors.

Then fill in one body at a time, running the tests after each.

topics.title: Two Pointers
topics.description: Converging and sliding indices for linear-time array and string evaluations.

exercises.title: Two Sum II - Input Array Is Sorted
Design an Opposite-Ends Window Tracker
exercises.time_complexity_target: O(1) end updates, O(W) pair-sum query

hints.title: Nudge
hints.content_markdown: The window must stay non-decreasing. Ask what that costs each time you extend an end, and what a query can then safely discard.

hints.title: Strategy
hints.content_markdown:
1. `push_left` accepts a value only when it is at or below the current front; `push_right` only when it is at or above the current back. Anything else throws `std::invalid_argument` and leaves the window untouched.
2. `shrink_left` / `shrink_right` drop an end and throw `std::out_of_range` when empty.
3. `contains(target)` sweeps inward: `lo` from the front, `hi` from the back. If the sum is too small, advance `lo`; if too large, retreat `hi`. Stop when `lo >= hi` so no position is used twice.

hints.title: Method blueprint
hints.content_markdown:
Signatures and invariants only:

- `OppositeEndsTracker()` / `OppositeEndsTracker(const std::vector<int>& initial)` -- reject an unsorted seed.
- `void push_left(int value)` / `void push_right(int value)` -- enforce the ordering precondition.
- `void shrink_left()` / `void shrink_right()` -- throw when empty.
- `bool contains(int target) const` -- the inward sweep; O(W).
- `int size() const` / `int at(int i) const` / `bool is_ordered() const` -- O(1).
- `void reset()` -- empties the window.

Write the pruning comment first; it is the part being tested.

topics.title: Sliding Window
topics.description: Dynamic and fixed windows maintaining state invariants across contiguous subranges.

exercises.title: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock

hints.title: Nudge
hints.content_markdown: Which quantities does the technique read off the window? Width, counts, and whether anything repeats -- and each must survive an end moving.

hints.title: Strategy
hints.content_markdown:
1. `push` raises `distinct` only the first time a value is seen, so read the count before incrementing it.
2. `pop` throws `std::out_of_range` when the value is absent. When a count reaches zero, erase the key and lower `distinct` -- forgetting this is the step that makes every later width comparison wrong.
3. `all_unique` is `distinct == size`. `max_count` scans the counts.
4. `clear` empties the map and resets both derived counters.

hints.title: Method blueprint
hints.content_markdown:
Signatures, no bodies:

- `SlidingWindow()` -- empty window.
- `void push(int value)` / `void pop(int value)` -- the O(1) end updates.
- `int size() const` / `int count_of(int value) const` / `int distinct() const` -- O(1) once `distinct` is maintained.
- `bool all_unique() const` / `int max_count() const` -- O(1) / O(D).
- `void clear()` -- resets everything.

topics.title: Stack
topics.description: Last-In First-Out (LIFO) tracking, expression evaluation, and monotonic stacks.

hints.title: Nudge
hints.content_markdown: `std::stack` cannot report full, because the vector underneath it grows. Fixing the capacity is what makes `empty` and `full` two distinct, reachable states.

hints.title: Strategy
hints.content_markdown:
1. Allocate a buffer of `capacity` slots in the constructor; a non-positive capacity becomes 1.
2. `push` throws `std::overflow_error` when full, else stores and raises the height.
3. `pop` and `peek` throw `std::out_of_range` when the height is 0. `pop` lowers the height; `peek` must not.
4. `clear` sets the height to 0 and leaves the buffer alone -- which is why `peek` afterwards throws instead of returning a stale element.
5. The destructor frees the buffer, and copying is deleted.

hints.title: Method blueprint
hints.content_markdown:
Signatures only:

- `explicit BoundedStack(int capacity)` / `~BoundedStack()` -- own the buffer; non-copyable.
- `void push(int value)` -- `std::overflow_error` when full.
- `int pop()` / `int peek() const` -- `std::out_of_range` when empty.
- `bool empty() const` / `bool full() const` -- mutually exclusive.
- `int size() const` / `int capacity() const` -- height and fixed bound.
- `void clear()` -- height only.

topics.title: Binary Search
topics.description: Logarithmic search space halving, sorted array queries, and predicate boundaries.

exercises.title: Find Minimum in Rotated Sorted Array

hints.title: Nudge
hints.content_markdown: Binary search answers boundary questions, not hit-or-miss ones. Get `lower_bound` right and `upper_bound` is the same loop with one comparison changed.

hints.title: Strategy
hints.content_markdown:
1. Sort on construction -- the search precondition is the structure's responsibility, not the caller's.
2. Both bounds use the closed half-open interval `[lo, hi)` with `hi = size()`. Probe `mid = lo + (hi - lo) / 2`.
3. `lower_bound`: move `lo` to `mid + 1` when `sorted[mid] < target`, otherwise `hi = mid`. `upper_bound` is identical except it uses `<=`.
4. `count_of` is the difference of the two bounds; `contains` checks that `lower_bound` actually lands on the target.
5. Never write `(lo + hi) / 2` -- it overflows near `INT_MAX`.

hints.title: Method blueprint
hints.content_markdown:
Signatures and invariants only:

- `explicit SearchIndex(std::vector<int> values)` -- sorts on entry.
- `int lower_bound(int target) const` -- first index not less than target, or `size()`.
- `int upper_bound(int target) const` -- first index greater than target, or `size()`.
- `int count_of(int target) const` -- difference of the two bounds.
- `bool contains(int target) const` -- one lookup, no second pass.
- `int at(int i) const` / `int size() const` / `int probe_count(int target) const` -- accessors and the halving counter.

topics.title: Linked Lists
topics.description: Pointer manipulation, node reversal, cycle detection, and list traversal.

hints.title: Node & Head Pointers
hints.content_markdown: Define a `ListNode` struct with `val` and `next`. Maintain a `head` pointer and an integer `size` in your `LinkedList` class.

hints.title: Edge Handling & Traversal
hints.content_markdown:
1. `insertHead`: allocate a new node, point its `next` to `head`, then update `head`.
2. `insertTail`: if `!head`, set `head = node`. Otherwise traverse until `curr->next == nullptr` and link.
3. `remove`: check `0 <= index < size`. For head removal, update `head = head->next`. For other positions, stop at `index - 1`, splice out `curr->next`, and `delete` the removed node.

hints.title: Complete Class Blueprint

exercises.title: Remove Nth Node From End of List
Design a Doubly Linked List
exercises.time_complexity_target: O(1) end updates, O(i) indexed access

hints.title: Nudge
hints.content_markdown: The `prev` pointer is what makes deleting a *known* node O(1). Every operation that changes the chain must therefore update two links, and a single missed re-link creates a cycle that nothing reports.

hints.title: Strategy
hints.content_markdown:
1. On an empty list the new node is both head and tail -- get that right in `push_front`, `push_back`, and in both `pop` methods.
2. `pop_front` advances `head` and clears the new `head->prev`; `pop_back` is the mirror. Each releases the detached node.
3. `at(i)` should walk from whichever end is nearer.
4. `reverse` swaps each node's `prev` and `next` in a single pass, then swaps head and tail. Both links must move together.
5. `is_consistent` walks both directions and confirms each `next->prev` points back, which is what makes the other tests meaningful.

hints.title: Method blueprint
hints.content_markdown:
Signatures and per-operation invariants:

- `DoublyLinkedList()` / `~DoublyLinkedList()` -- non-copyable.
- `void push_front(int)` / `void push_back(int)` -- O(1).
- `int pop_front()` / `int pop_back()` -- `std::out_of_range` when empty.
- `int at(int i) const` -- `std::out_of_range` unless in range.
- `void insert_after(int i, int value)` / `void erase_after(int i)` -- splice and unlink, moving the tail when needed.
- `bool contains(int value) const` / `int size() const` / `bool empty() const` / `bool is_consistent() const`.
- `void clear()` / `void reverse()`.

topics.title: Trees & Binary Search Trees
topics.description: Recursive tree traversals, structural inversions, depths, and search properties.

exercises.title: Lowest Common Ancestor of a Binary Search Tree
Design a Binary Search Tree
exercises.time_complexity_target: O(H) per operation, H the height

hints.title: Nudge
hints.content_markdown: One rule defines the structure: every key left of a node is smaller, every key right of it is larger. `inorder` is that rule written down -- if it stops being sorted, a mutation broke it.

hints.title: Strategy
hints.content_markdown:
1. `insert` descends left for a smaller key, right for a larger one, and does nothing for an equal key -- the tree is a set.
2. `contains`, `find_min`, and `find_max` are pure descents; the last two throw `std::out_of_range` on an empty tree.
3. `remove` has three cases. No left child: promote the right. No right child: promote the left. **Two** children: copy the inorder successor's key in, then delete the successor from the right subtree.
4. `height` is 0 when empty and 1 + the larger child height otherwise. Insert sorted keys and it becomes N -- that contrast is the lesson.

hints.title: Method blueprint
hints.content_markdown:
Signatures and the invariant each one preserves:

- `BST()` / `~BST()` -- non-copyable, releases the subtree.
- `void insert(int key)` -- duplicates ignored.
- `bool contains(int key) const` / `int find_min() const` / `int find_max() const` -- descents; the extremes throw when empty.
- `void remove(int key)` -- the three cases above; absent keys are a no-op.
- `int size() const` / `int height() const` / `std::vector<int> inorder() const` -- left, node, right.
- `void clear()`.

topics.title: Tries (Prefix Trees)
topics.description: Multi-way branching prefix trees for string retrieval and dictionary autocomplete.

exercises.title: Design Add and Search Words Data Structure
Design a Prefix Trie
exercises.time_complexity_target: O(L) per operation, L the word length

hints.title: Nudge
hints.content_markdown: The fixed 26-slot fan-out is what removes hashing from a walk -- but it only works for lowercase letters, and it is that domain check that keeps the array index in bounds.

hints.title: Strategy
hints.content_markdown:
1. `c - 'a'` is sound only for `'a'..'z'`. For a digit the difference is negative, and indexing a 26-slot array with it is undefined behaviour that aborts rather than answers. Validate the whole word *before* descending, so a bad word cannot leave a half-built chain.
2. `search` needs the final node to exist **and** carry the word-ending mark; `starts_with` needs only the path.
3. `remove` clears the mark, then prunes bottom-up, stopping as soon as a node has children or is itself a word ending. Both conditions matter.
4. Keep `node_total` exact in step with the pruning.

hints.title: Method blueprint
hints.content_markdown:
Signatures and the precondition each one enforces:

- `Trie()` -- one node, the empty prefix.
- `void insert(const std::string& word)` -- ignore out-of-domain input; duplicates change nothing.
- `bool search(const std::string&) const` / `bool starts_with(const std::string&) const` -- O(L).
- `bool remove(const std::string& word)` -- false when absent or out-of-domain.
- `int size() const` / `int node_total() const` / `int height() const`.
- `static int slot_of(char c)` -- the domain guard everything else uses.

topics.title: Heap & Priority Queue
topics.description: Logarithmic min/max tracking, stream percentiles, and top-k selection.

exercises.title: Kth Largest Element in a Stream
Kth Largest Element in an Array
Design a Binary Max-Heap
exercises.time_complexity_target: O(log N) push and pop, O(N) build

hints.title: Nudge
hints.content_markdown: The layout rule is the whole structure: the node at index `i` has children at `2i + 1` and `2i + 2`. Get that arithmetic wrong and you get something that looks like a heap and is not.

hints.title: Strategy
hints.content_markdown:
1. `push` appends, then sifts the new last index up. Sifting moves the held value one level per step and never revisits a level -- that is the O(log N).
2. `pop` returns the root, moves the last element there, shrinks, and sifts the root down. It throws `std::out_of_range` when empty.
3. `build` must sift down only the **internal** nodes, from `(n - 2) / 2` up to 0. Inserting one at a time instead is O(N log N) and an easy regression.
4. `contains` is a linear scan. A heap orders parents against children, not values against each other, so there is nothing to binary search.

hints.title: Method blueprint
hints.content_markdown:
Signatures and the arithmetic:

- `explicit BinaryHeap(int initial_capacity = 4)` / `void build(std::vector<int> values)` -- bulk construction in O(N).
- `void push(int value)` / `int pop()` / `int peek() const` -- O(log N), O(1), O(log N).
- `void sift_up(int index)` / `void sift_down(int index)` -- children at `2i+1`/`2i+2`, parent at `(i-1)/2`.
- `int size() const` / `bool empty() const` / `bool contains(int) const` -- `contains` is O(N), deliberately.
- `bool is_valid() const` / `void clear()` / `std::vector<int> drain()`.

Write `is_valid` first; it is what tells you the rest works.

topics.title: Backtracking
topics.description: Exhaustive depth-first search exploring decision trees with branch pruning.

exercises.title: Design a Backtracking Choice Stack
exercises.time_complexity_target: O(1) amortized undo, expected O(1) memo lookup

hints.title: Nudge
hints.content_markdown: Backtracking is not 'try a candidate' -- it is 'try, and put everything back'. Making the undo countable is most of what this structure is for.

hints.title: Strategy
hints.content_markdown:
1. `pop_choice` undoes one level and counts it, so `backtrack_count` is a direct readout of discarded work.
2. The memo key must combine the current path **and** the candidate. Hashing only the candidate makes one depth's refusal poison another's, and the search returns wrong answers.
3. `tried_at_current_depth` must count branches refused *at* this depth. A descendant's key also starts with this path's text, so a prefix match alone reports a child's refusals as the parent's.
4. `reset` clears the branch, the refusals, and the counter.

hints.title: Method blueprint
hints.content_markdown:
Signatures and the key's contract:

- `ChoiceStack()` -- empty branch, nothing refused.
- `void push_choice(int choice)` / `int pop_choice()` -- O(1) amortized; `pop_choice` throws on an empty branch.
- `int depth() const` / `int at(int i) const` -- O(1).
- `bool tried(int candidate) const` / `void mark_tried(int candidate)` -- key on path plus candidate.
- `int tried_at_current_depth() const` -- exact depth only.
- `bool is_backtracking() const` / `int backtrack_count() const` / `void reset()` -- counters.

topics.title: Graphs
topics.description: Node connectivity, grid flood fills, topological traversals, and cycle detection.

hints.title: Nudge
hints.content_markdown: An adjacency matrix costs O(V^2) whether or not edges exist; a list costs O(V + E) and is why a traversal is linear in the graph. The price is that `has_edge` is O(deg(u)) rather than O(1) -- say so rather than hide it.

hints.title: Strategy
hints.content_markdown:
1. Store each edge as a `(neighbour, weight)` pair at **both** endpoints. A separate weight table has to be index-aligned with the adjacency lists, and the alignment breaks the first time an edge is removed from the middle of one.
2. `add_edge` on an existing pair updates the weight instead of duplicating. A self-loop is recorded once, so `degree` counts it once.
3. `remove_edge` must drop both sides and lower the edge count; removing an absent edge is a no-op.
4. `is_symmetric` is the bug catcher: a one-sided insert makes a traversal silently miss half the graph.

hints.title: Method blueprint
hints.content_markdown:
Signatures and the representation:

- `explicit AdjacencyGraph(int vertex_limit)` -- clamp a non-positive limit to 0.
- `int vertex_count() const` / `long long edge_count() const` / `void add_vertex()`.
- `void add_edge(int u, int v, long long weight = 1)` / `bool has_edge(int u, int v) const` / `long long weight_between(int u, int v) const`.
- `int degree(int u) const` / `std::vector<int> neighbours_of(int u) const` / `std::vector<int> sorted_neighbours(int u) const`.
- `void remove_edge(int u, int v)` / `bool is_symmetric() const` / `bool is_simple() const`.

Document the storage as one entry per incident edge.

topics.title: Dynamic Programming
topics.description: Optimal substructure, memoization, bottom-up tabulation, and state transitions.

hints.title: Nudge
hints.content_markdown: Memoisation is one sentence: compute a state once, then read it back. The payoff depends entirely on *when* the store is consulted relative to the work.

hints.title: Strategy
hints.content_markdown:
1. Consult `is_computed` **before** computing. Read after, and every path reaching a state re-walks its subtree -- the exponential behaviour memoisation exists to remove.
2. A missing key must be distinguishable from a computed `0`, or every subproblem looks already solved. `get` throws; `get_or` substitutes an explicit fallback.
3. Count every read. A table whose hit count stays at zero while a long computation finishes is not memoising anything, however correct the answer.
4. `clear` keeps the counters, `reset` zeroes them. That distinction is what lets you compare two runs.

hints.title: Method blueprint
hints.content_markdown:
Signatures and the ordering contract:

- `MemoTable()` -- empty, no reads recorded.
- `bool is_computed(long long key) const` -- checked before the work.
- `long long get(long long key) const` -- throws `std::out_of_range` on a miss, and counts it.
- `long long get_or(long long key, long long fallback) const` -- counts the miss too.
- `void set(long long key, long long value)` -- re-storing adds no entry.
- `int size() const` / `long long hits() const` / `long long misses() const`.
- `void clear()` / `void reset()` / `std::vector<long long> keys() const` -- sorted with an O(K log K) sort.

topics.title: Sorting
topics.description: Comparison and counting sorts, their invariants, and the lower bound that separates them from everything else.

exercises.title: Design a Bottom-Up Merge Sort
exercises.time_complexity_target: O(N log N), O(N) per merge pass

hints.title: Nudge
hints.content_markdown: Merge sort's unit of work is the sorted **run**. Make the runs countable and the algorithm's state becomes visible instead of hidden behind a call stack.

hints.title: Strategy
hints.content_markdown:
1. A run ends wherever the sequence stops ascending. Compare with `<`, not `<=`, so equal neighbours stay in one run; a sorted array is then exactly one run.
2. Merge with `<=` on the left half, or equal elements lose their relative order and the sort stops being stable.
3. In the lane loop, after merging runs `i` and `i+1` the merged run **occupies index `i`**, so the next partner is at `i + 1` and the loop must advance by one. Advancing by two skips a pair, each pass stops halving, and the pass count exceeds ceil(log2 R) -- still correct, quietly slower.
4. `passes()` is the ceil(log2 R) the cost argument derives.

hints.title: Method blueprint
hints.content_markdown:
Signatures and the run representation:

- `explicit MergeSorter(std::vector<int> initial)` -- holds the values.
- `void build()` -- records maximal ascending runs as half-open `[begin, end)` ranges.
- `int count_runs() const` / `int run_length(int i) const` / `int run_start(int i) const` -- run inspection.
- `void merge_two_runs(int i)` / `void merge_all()` / `void sort()`.
- `int passes() const` / `long long comparison_count() const` -- the two halves of the cost argument, counted.
- `bool is_sorted() const` / `int at(int i) const` / `int size() const` / `void reset()` / `void set_values(std::vector<int>)`.

topics.title: Graph Algorithms
topics.description: Traversal, topological order, and shortest paths, with the cost derivation for each and the conditions that make them sound.

exercises.title: Design a Breadth-First Frontier
exercises.time_complexity_target: O(1) per operation, O(V + E) per traversal

hints.title: Nudge
hints.content_markdown: Mark a vertex visited when it is **enqueued**, not when it is dequeued. Break that and a vertex reachable by two parents is queued twice, expanded twice, and its whole subtree walked twice -- with no crash and no wrong answer.

hints.title: Strategy
hints.content_markdown:
1. `enqueue` returns false without queueing anything when the vertex is already visited. That single check is what keeps the frontier linear.
2. Keep a cursor rather than erasing from the front, so `pending()` is a contiguous range instead of a per-operation shift.
3. `enqueued_count` versus `vertex_count` is the readout: under mark-on-enqueue they are equal; under mark-on-dequeue the insertions run to O(E).
4. `is_complete` is true when nothing is waiting -- not when nothing was ever enqueued. A search can drain and then be extended again.

hints.title: Method blueprint
hints.content_markdown:
Signatures and the discovery rule:

- `explicit BfsFrontier(int vertex_count = 0)` -- empty.
- `bool enqueue(int vertex)` -- mark, queue, count; false if already visited.
- `int dequeue()` / `int peek() const` -- oldest first; throw `std::out_of_range` when empty.
- `bool is_visited(int) const` / `int frontier_size() const` / `std::vector<int> pending() const`.
- `int expanded_count() const` / `int vertex_count() const` / `long long enqueued_count() const`.
- `bool is_complete() const` / `void reset()`.

topics.title: Advanced Data Structures
topics.description: Disjoint-set union, segment trees, and Fenwick trees: structures that answer range questions in logarithmic time.

hints.title: Nudge
hints.content_markdown: Two optimisations, and both are needed. Path compression flattens the trees during `find`; union by rank stops long chains forming in the first place. Together they reach the inverse-Ackermann bound.

hints.title: Strategy
hints.content_markdown:
1. `find` walks to the root, then walks again rewriting every node on the path to point straight at it. The second pass is what makes a *sequence* of calls cheap rather than each call in isolation.
2. `unite` attaches the lower-rank root under the higher-rank one and bumps the rank only when the ranks were equal. Attaching by element id instead produces a linear chain the moment ids arrive ascending, and every `find` becomes O(N) while still returning the right answer.
3. Nothing about correctness distinguishes a healthy structure from a degenerate one. `tree_height` does: bounded by ceil(log2 N) when the rank rule is in force, and near N when it is missing.

hints.title: Method blueprint
hints.content_markdown:
Signatures and the two optimisations:

- `explicit UnionFind(int element_count)` -- one set per element; clamp a negative count to 0.
- `int find(int element)` -- path-compressing root lookup; throws `std::out_of_range`.
- `bool unite(int a, int b)` -- false when already in one set.
- `bool connected(int a, int b)` / `int component_count() const` / `int rank_of_set(int element)`.
- `int tree_height()` -- the diagnostic for a degenerate structure.
- `void reset()` / `void split(int element)` -- `split` throws `std::logic_error`: a disjoint set cannot lose one element.

topics.title: Math and Bitwise Techniques
topics.description: Bit identities, XOR properties, and mask arithmetic — the arithmetic that makes constant-time tricks possible.

hints.title: Nudge
hints.content_markdown: Membership is a shift and a mask against one word: no allocation, no branch, no memory access beyond the word. That is also why subset, superset, disjoint, and overlap all reduce to `&` between two masks.

hints.title: Strategy
hints.content_markdown:
1. Build every mask from `1ULL`. `1 << 31` is already undefined behaviour on a 32-bit `int`, and `1 << 32` is meaningless -- so range-check the position and use the wide literal.
2. An all-ones mask avoids shifting by the width: compute it as `width >= 64 ? ~0ULL : (1ULL << width) - 1`.
3. `count` uses Kernighan's trick -- `bits &= bits - 1` clears the lowest set bit -- so the loop runs once per set bit, not once per bit.
4. `resize` must refuse to narrow past a set bit. Discarding it silently loses data behind a successful return.

hints.title: Method blueprint
hints.content_markdown:
Signatures and the two arithmetic hazards:

- `explicit BitMaskSet(int bit_width = 0)` -- clamp to `[0, MAX_WIDTH]`.
- `void set(int)` / `void clear(int)` / `void flip(int)` / `bool contains(int) const` -- bounds-checked, mask from `1ULL`.
- `int count() const` -- Kernighan's trick.
- `unsigned long long to_mask() const` / `int bit_width() const`.
- `bool any() const` / `bool all() const` -- a zero-width set is vacuously full.
- `void reset()` / `void set_all()` / `void resize(int)` -- narrowing throws `std::logic_error` past a set bit.
- `std::string to_string() const` -- most significant bit first.
